stimulus.text: A printer prints pages at a constant rate. The table shows the total number of pages the printer has printed after various amounts of time.

stem: At this rate, how many pages will the printer print in 20 minutes?
rationale: The rate is constant, so any row of the table gives the unit rate: \(7\) pages in \(4\) minutes is \(\frac{7}{4}\) pages per minute (the other rows confirm it: \(14/8 = 21/12 = 7/4\)). Set up the proportion with matching unit positions: \(\frac{7 \text{ pages}}{4 \text{ minutes}} = \frac{x \text{ pages}}{20 \text{ minutes}}\). Cross-multiplying gives \(4x = 140\), so \(x = 35\) pages. Check by the alternate path: \(\frac{7}{4} \times 20 = 35\), and the direction makes sense — more minutes must mean more pages. A student with the cross-multiplication-misalignment bug would write \(\frac{4}{7} = \frac{x}{20}\), pairing minutes with pages across the equals sign, and get \(\frac{80}{7} \approx 11.4\) — the reciprocated setup. A part-whole confusion might lead a student to treat 20 minutes as an extension of the 12-minute row and just add 7 to 21, getting 28, but that wrongly assumes 8 more minutes produces only one more 4-minute batch's worth of pages without scaling. Because the unit rate \(\frac{7}{4}\) is not a whole number, mental multiplication fails; the proportion must be solved exactly, which is why the correct answer is 35.
